title: THE QUEEN WHO CAME TO BREAK SOLOMON WITH HARD QUESTIONS—Then Left Behind a Fortune
paragraphs: THE QUEEN WHO CAME TO BREAK SOLOMON WITH HARD QUESTIONS—Then Left Behind a Fortune

She crossed a world to test the wisest king alive. She carried questions she refused to leave unanswered. But nearly a thousand years later, Jesus revealed the part of her story that should make every comfortable Christian tremble: she traveled desperately for wisdom while the world’s true King can be standing right in front of us—and we can still refuse to listen.
There are questions you ask because you are curious.
And then there are questions you carry because something inside you is bleeding.
Questions you rehearse when nobody is around.
Questions about God.
About suffering.
About the prayer that still has not been answered.
About why the person you loved was taken.
About why God allowed the betrayal.
About why you keep falling into the same sin after promising Him you would never go back.
About why heaven sometimes seems painfully quiet.
Maybe that is why the opening of 1 Kings 10 feels so strangely human.
A queen heard a rumor.
Somewhere beyond her own kingdom, there was a man unlike ordinary men.
His name was Solomon.
And the reports surrounding him had become impossible to ignore.
But the biblical text gives us a detail that changes the atmosphere of the entire encounter:
וּמַלְכַּת־שְׁבָא שֹׁמַעַת אֶת־שֵׁמַע שְׁלֹמֹה לְשֵׁם יְהוָה וַתָּבֹא לְנַסֹּתוֹ בְּחִידוֹת
U-malkat Sheva shoma'at et-shema Shelomoh le-shem YHWH, va-tavo lenassoto beḥidot.
The Queen of Sheba heard of Solomon's fame in connection with the name of the LORD, and she came to test him with hard questions.
Look closely at those final Hebrew words.
לְנַסֹּתוֹ — lenassoto.
To test him.
To prove him.
To put what she had heard to the test.
And then:
בְּחִידוֹת — beḥidot.
Riddles. Enigmas. Difficult questions.
She wasn't traveling all that distance for small talk.
She came carrying questions.
And maybe that is where her ancient story suddenly becomes yours.
Because perhaps you came to God carrying some too.
The Queen of Sheba arrived in Jerusalem with an enormous entourage. Camels carried spices, precious stones, and a staggering quantity of gold.
But underneath all that royal magnificence was something money could not purchase:
answers.
Scripture says something remarkably intimate about what happened when she finally stood before Solomon.
וַתְּדַבֵּר אֵלָיו אֵת כָּל־אֲשֶׁר הָיָה עִם־לְבָבָהּ
She spoke to him about all that was in her heart.
All of it.
Imagine that moment.
The servants disappear into the background.
The camels no longer matter.
The gold does not matter.
The jewels do not matter.
One human being finally begins emptying what she has carried inside.
Maybe you know that feeling.
You can look successful and still carry questions.
You can have money and still ache.
You can lead people and still be confused.
You can post smiling photographs while privately asking God why your life feels like it is collapsing.
You can sit in church, sing every lyric, lift your hands, say “Amen,” and still have something buried deep inside your heart that you are almost afraid to say aloud.
The Queen of Sheba reminds us that possessing much does not mean needing nothing.
And Scripture says Solomon answered her.
Nothing she brought before him was beyond his God-given wisdom.
Then she began looking around.
She saw his wisdom.
His house.
His table.
His servants.
Their organization.
Their clothing.
His worship.
The entire kingdom testified that what she had heard was not exaggeration.
And 1 Kings records an extraordinary Hebrew expression:
וְלֹא־הָיָה בָהּ עוֹד רוּחַ
Ve-lo hayah vah od ruaḥ.
Literally, there was no more breath/spirit in her.
She was overwhelmed.
Breathless.
The woman who came to examine Solomon suddenly found herself astonished by what she encountered.
She admitted that she had heard the reports back home...
but she had not believed them.
Not fully.
Not until she came.
Not until she saw.
Not until she heard.
And then she essentially confessed:
I wasn't told the half of it.
But here is where Christians can easily stop the story too early.
We can turn 1 Kings 10 into a story about prosperity.
Gold.
Success.
Royalty.
Wisdom.
Influence.
We can stare at Solomon's throne so long that we miss the road leading from Jerusalem to Jesus Christ.
Because centuries later, Jesus Himself brought this woman back into the story.
He called her “the queen of the south.”
And Christ said that she would rise in the judgment with His generation because she came from far away to hear Solomon's wisdom.
Then Jesus delivered the sentence that changes how Christians must read the entire encounter:
καὶ ἰδοὺ πλεῖον Σολομῶνος ὧδε
Kai idou, pleion Solomōnos hōde.
“Behold... something greater than Solomon is here.”
Greater than Solomon.
Stop there.
Because suddenly Solomon is no longer the destination.
He becomes a signpost.
The queen traveled an extraordinary distance to hear the wisdom of a mortal king.
But the eternal Son of God came to us.
Solomon could answer riddles.
Jesus answers humanity's deepest problem.
Solomon possessed wisdom.
Christ is the One in whom the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are found.
Solomon sat on an earthly throne.
Jesus reigns as King of kings.
Solomon received extravagant gifts.
Jesus gave Himself.
Solomon could tell a troubled woman what she wanted to know.
Jesus can take a condemned sinner and make that sinner new.
And that is where this story stops being comfortable.
Because the Queen of Sheba crossed enormous distance for lesser wisdom.
How far are we willing to go for Christ?
We have Bibles within arm's reach.
Sermons available in seconds.
Scripture on our phones.
Churches nearby.
Devotionals everywhere.
We can hear the Gospel while lying in bed.
Yet sometimes a woman from the ancient world seems more desperate to hear wisdom than people who possess immediate access to the words of Jesus Christ.
She traveled.
We scroll.
She searched.
We swipe.
She questioned.
We distract ourselves.
She brought everything that was in her heart.
We hide everything in ours.
And perhaps the hardest question in 1 Kings 10 is not one the Queen of Sheba asked Solomon.
Perhaps the hardest question is the one her journey asks us:
If she went that far for Solomon, what excuse do we have for remaining spiritually indifferent to Jesus?
That hurts.
Because some of us are not rejecting Jesus loudly.
We are simply postponing Him quietly.
Tomorrow I'll pray.
Tomorrow I'll repent.
Tomorrow I'll forgive.
Tomorrow I'll stop.
Tomorrow I'll open my Bible.
Tomorrow I'll return to church.
Tomorrow I'll surrender this relationship.
Tomorrow I'll confess what I've hidden.
Tomorrow I'll become serious about Christ.
Tomorrow.
Tomorrow.
Tomorrow.
Until “tomorrow” becomes ten years.
And meanwhile the heart becomes increasingly skilled at living without surrender.
That may be one of the most dangerous spiritual conditions imaginable.
Not hatred of God.
Familiarity with God without obedience to Him.
Knowing Christian language without knowing surrender.
Knowing Bible verses while protecting secret sin.
Knowing how to look alive while slowly becoming numb inside.
The Queen of Sheba came with hard questions.
Maybe you should too.
God, why am I really running from You?
Why do I keep returning to what destroys me?
Why do I want forgiveness without repentance?
Why do I want Your blessings while resisting Your authority?
Why am I more concerned about what people think of me than what You see in me?
Why can I spend hours consuming entertainment and then claim I have no time for Scripture?
Why do I keep pretending I'm okay?
Those are uncomfortable questions.
But grace is not afraid of uncomfortable questions.
Jesus never needed you to clean up the evidence before approaching Him.
The Gospel is not the story of respectable people impressing God.
It is the announcement that sinners who could never rescue themselves can be forgiven because Jesus Christ came for them.
We sinned.
Christ came.
We deserved judgment.
Christ bore sin.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
The scandal is that guilty people can receive grace.
The miracle is that grace does not merely excuse us and leave us where it found us.
Grace calls us out.
Grace cleanses.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace restores.
Grace transforms.
Grace takes people with histories they cannot erase and gives them futures their failures could never manufacture.
Maybe you are reading this with a chapter of your life you desperately wish could be deleted.
An affair.
An addiction.
A lie.
A betrayal.
A secret.
A season of rebellion.
Years wasted.
Someone you hurt.
Something you watched.
Something you did when nobody knew.
Something that still makes you wonder whether God could possibly want you.
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending sin never mattered.
He rewrites sinners by paying sin's terrible price Himself and giving repentant people what they could never earn:
forgiveness.
The cross proves both how serious your sin is...
and how astonishing His mercy is.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not “keep living however you want” grace.
Transforming grace.
Grace that finds Peter after denial.
Grace that meets persecutors and creates apostles.
Grace that welcomes prodigals home.
Grace that tells sinners the truth and then offers them cleansing.
Grace with nail scars.
So bring the hard question.
Bring the shame.
Bring the anger.
Bring the doubt.
Bring what is in your heart.
But don't merely come looking for an explanation.
Come looking for Christ.
Because there are questions God may not answer the way you want.
There are mysteries you may carry for years.
Christian faith does not promise that every “why” will receive a complete explanation on this side of eternity.
It promises something greater.
Someone.
Jesus Christ.
And sometimes what your shattered heart needs most is not an explanation of every chapter.
It needs to know who is holding the book.
The Queen of Sheba eventually did something remarkable.
After hearing Solomon's wisdom and witnessing what God had done, she blessed the LORD.
She recognized that Solomon's throne ultimately testified to God's love and purposes.
Then came the gift.
One hundred and twenty talents of gold.
Spices in extraordinary abundance.
Precious stones.
An enormous act of generosity.
But Scripture never teaches that she purchased God's favor with those treasures.
Her giving came after encountering what had already astonished her.
That distinction matters.
Biblical generosity must never become spiritual commerce.
We do not purchase salvation.
We do not buy God's love.
We do not bribe heaven.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
“By grace are ye saved through faith... it is the gift of God.”
Christian giving, at its healthiest, flows from gratitude, worship, love, and a willing heart.
And this is why I want to speak plainly to those who believe Gospel Warrior should continue reaching people.
If these articles have helped bring you back to Scripture...
if they have confronted something you were hiding...
if they have encouraged you on nights when your faith felt exhausted...
if they have helped you speak about Jesus with someone you love...
then you can become part of keeping this mission moving.
It does not.
It does not.
And not because God needs our money.
He does not.
But Gospel ministry in the real world requires people willing to give, serve, create, share, encourage, and support.
But please hear this:
The greatest reward is not merchandise.
It is not a discount.
It is not recognition.
It is knowing that what God has placed in your hands can be used to help put Gospel truth in front of another human heart.
And there is another way you can help that costs nothing.
That simple share matters more than you may realize.
Someone quietly losing a battle.
Someone smiling publicly and breaking privately.
Someone who stopped praying.
Someone ashamed to return to church.
Someone wondering whether Jesus could still forgive them.
Someone who would never tell you how close they are to giving up.
You may never know what happens after you press “Share.”
Not to make us famous.
Make Jesus known.
And if this article found the part of you that you normally keep hidden, don't disappear silently.
There is no shame in needing prayer.

And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell us. Your testimony may become the sentence another struggling believer desperately needed to read tonight.
Because there will be another night when the questions return.
Another disappointment.
Another prayer that seems unanswered.
Another moment when your feelings begin preaching louder than Scripture.
Come back and remember:
The Queen of Sheba brought her hard questions.
You can bring yours.
But you have access to Someone infinitely greater than Solomon.
Read.
Study.
Test what you hear against Scripture.
Grow.
Pray.
Repent when the Word exposes you.
Encourage someone else.
And keep returning to Jesus.
Because eventually every earthly treasure stays behind.
The Queen of Sheba's gold did.
Solomon's palace did.
His throne did.
His astonishing wealth did.
Kingdoms rise.
Fortunes change hands.
Famous names become chapters in history books.
But Christ remains.
And perhaps this ancient queen leaves us with one final picture.
She came carrying treasure.
But she was searching for wisdom.
She came prepared to test a king.
But she left praising the King who had given Solomon his wisdom.
Then centuries passed.
Another King appeared.
No caravan announced Him.
No mountain of gold surrounded His birth.
He entered our world in humility.
He touched lepers.
Welcomed outcasts.
Confronted hypocrites.
Forgave sinners.
Called people to repentance.
Carried a cross.
And wore a crown made of thorns.
Solomon's visitors came bearing gold.
Jesus came bearing our sin.
Solomon answered difficult questions.
Jesus answered humanity's condemnation with His own blood.
Solomon amazed a queen.
Jesus walked out of a grave.
And now the question has crossed thousands of years and arrived in front of you.
Not:
What would you have asked Solomon?
But:
What will you do with Jesus?
You can admire Him and remain unchanged.
You can read about Him and never surrender.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still keep the throne of your heart for yourself.
Or you can finally stop hiding.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
Bring Him the questions.
Bring Him the wounds.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the ruined chapter.
Bring Him the life you cannot repair.
And discover that the Savior who already knows the worst thing about you is still calling sinners to come.
The Queen of Sheba traveled far because she heard there was wisdom in Jerusalem.
You don't have to cross a desert.
But you may have to cross your pride.
You may have to cross your shame.
You may have to cross years of excuses.
You may have to finally surrender the thing you keep protecting from God.
Come.
Not to Solomon.
To the One greater than Solomon.
Come to Jesus.
Because after all the hard questions have been asked, all the earthly treasures have changed hands, and every human kingdom has disappeared into history, one truth will still remain:
You may have spent years wondering whether Jesus could rewrite your story, while all along He was waiting for you to finally stop hiding the page.
